title: Broadly transferable perennial grain production

concept.text: The innovation would be a broadly transferable way to breed or engineer grain crops that survive harvest, regrow and produce useful grain yields for several years from one planting. It would combine reliable plant persistence with repeated seed production, so farmers could harvest successive crops without establishing a new stand each season. Productive perennial rice already provides a substantial example; the broader ambition is to make this capability reproducible across major grain crops and contrasting production environments.

The proposed capability concerns a coordinated biological and agricultural system: plants must survive between harvests, retain the capacity to regrow, flower successfully and fill grain while remaining manageable in the field. It does not require indefinite survival or a single conserved, reversible genetic master switch. Such a switch is an unproven hypothesis in the supplied evidence, while the rice demonstration shows that multigeneration breeding can produce useful perenniality without establishing that mechanism.

significance.text: If productive perenniality became transferable across major grains and environments, it could substantially change how often farmers must establish crops and disturb soil. In the reported rice system, regrowth removes the need to repeat seedling nurseries, ploughing and transplanting for every harvest. Extending comparable advantages to other crops could reduce establishment work and associated costs, although the particular operations avoided would depend on the local annual production system.

Longer-lived stands could also change erosion, soil carbon, input requirements and farm labor. These are conditional consequences rather than automatic benefits of perenniality. Crop characteristics, climate, water management, disease pressure and the annual system being replaced would determine their magnitude and sometimes their direction. Establishment savings must be assessed alongside any additional management required to maintain productive stands.

Soil carbon accumulation alone would not establish a net climate benefit. The rice study identifies methane and nitrous oxide emissions, and their dependence on management, as important unresolved parts of the greenhouse-gas balance. Likewise, findings from irrigated rice cannot by themselves establish erosion protection, input savings or economic gains across other grain systems. The transformative prospect is wider access to productive multiyear cultivation; universal environmental superiority is not established.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this proposed innovation is reliable transfer: developing productive perennial grains across crops and environments with sufficiently predictable breeding, engineering and management methods. The supplied rice result establishes a valuable baseline, but does not demonstrate a general recipe that produces comparable persistence and yield across crop families. The supplied record also does not establish how much subsequent work has narrowed that gap.

Biologically, successful perennial grain production requires survival, regrowth, spikelet fertility and grain yield to remain compatible over successive harvests. Plants must support seed production while retaining the resources and living tissues needed for another growth cycle. The study discusses assimilate reserves, but the supplied review does not identify a direct quantitative measurement of the trade-off between seed production and storage. That allocation problem is therefore a plausible research barrier, not a demonstrated universal constraint with an established numerical relationship.

Persistence also has climatic and biological limits. Winter cold, summer heat and drought can reduce regrowth or kill plants. Maintaining a stand across seasons can carry diseases forward and change weed-management demands. Breeding must therefore be integrated with plant pathology and agronomy, including decisions about when declining stands should be replaced. Extending productive stand life indefinitely is unnecessary; the practical challenge is to sustain useful performance long enough for the system's benefits to outweigh its costs.

current_state.text: The study “Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice,” published online on 7 November 2022, reported irrigated trials in Yunnan during 2016–2020. From one planting, perennial rice produced eight consecutive harvests over four years. Reported average grain yield per harvest was 6.8 Mg ha−1 for perennial rice and 6.7 Mg ha−1 for replanted local annual comparators. These are yields per harvest, not annual totals. The result establishes that productive perennial staple rice was already a substantial demonstrated achievement.

The averages do not imply equal performance at every site or in every season. Performance varied by site, and grain yield decreased significantly in the fifth year, covering the ninth and tenth seasons. The four-year result therefore supports a bounded period of sustained production, not indefinite high yields. The adjacent-plot comparison design and the reported irrigated setting also limit extrapolation to other management systems, crops and climates.

The study also assessed labor requirements, input costs, returns and soil outcomes. Its explanation of avoided establishment operations provides a concrete basis for potential labor and tillage savings. These measurements make the demonstration broader than a finding that plants can merely survive harvest, but they do not establish that every perennial grain would deliver the same economic or environmental outcomes.

The supplied review assessed a partial representation of the paper containing the main article text and extended-data captions. Missing visual content, pages without extracted text and unavailable supplementary tables prevented independent reconstruction of the full results. These access limitations constrain verification of detailed analyses; they do not show that the reported results are false. No subsequent research record was supplied, so progress after this dated demonstration, including the field's position through 1 November 2026, remains unassessed.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently show a transferable breeding or engineering approach in multiple major grain crops spanning more than one crop family and contrasting production environments. The approach should explain which elements transfer between crops and which require crop-specific adaptation. Success in several closely related crops alone would provide narrower evidence than the cross-family ambition. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Transferable approaches demonstrated across crop families and contrasting production environments

completion_criteria.text: Proposed field evaluation: use replicated multiyear trials with locally appropriate annual comparators, reporting grain yield per harvest, total production over the full trial, survival, regrowth, fertility and stand replacement. Report site and season variation alongside averages, and follow stands long enough to characterize meaningful declines in productivity. Comparisons should include establishment and replacement costs so that a favorable early period does not obscure later losses.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated multiyear trials report comparative agronomic performance and full-trial costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical evaluation: measure labor, water, fertilizer and other relevant inputs, disease and weed management, soil outcomes and farm economics. Environmental claims should be tested directly: soil carbon measurements alone should not substitute for an assessment of the relevant greenhouse-gas balance, and erosion benefits should be demonstrated in the systems where they are claimed. Practical success should identify where perennial cultivation is advantageous and where annual production remains preferable.
completion_criteria.label: Measured practical and environmental outcomes establish where perennial cultivation benefits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: independent teams should reproduce the approach and its principal agronomic results using sufficiently documented breeding materials or engineering methods, field protocols and accessible outcome data. Demonstrations should state their tested climates, soils, crop backgrounds and management boundaries. A finite set of successful trials would establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality, and neither a universal molecular switch nor endless stand survival would be required.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce principal agronomic results within stated boundaries

related_concepts.text: Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: BOT-10, “Plants that reliably deposit durable additional carbon in soil,” overlaps with the possible soil effects of perennial grains, but asks for a distinct outcome. Repeated grain production from persistent plants does not establish durable additional carbon storage, and carbon storage would not by itself demonstrate productive perenniality or a favorable overall greenhouse-gas balance.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: BOT-08, “Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens,” and BOT-07, “Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops,” address stresses that can constrain multiyear stands. Better immunity or desiccation tolerance could support persistence, but each remains distinct from maintaining grain yield across repeated regrowth cycles. Perennial grain production does not inherently require resurrection-like tolerance.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” could help introduce and test candidate traits across crops. BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” could help anticipate interactions among regrowth, survival and yield. These are enabling capabilities; neither alone establishes successful perennial grain production under field conditions.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: BOT-06, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major crop families,” concerns how offspring inherit a parental genotype through seed. BOT-15 concerns repeated production by an established plant or stand. Clonal seed reproduction could help distribute a successful perennial variety, but it does not itself produce perenniality. BOT-14, “Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits,” likewise concerns inheritance across generations rather than the persistence of a stand across harvests.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: BOT-01, “Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops,” and BOT-16, “Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange,” could affect nutrition and input requirements in perennial systems. Their targets are nutrient acquisition and exchange, while BOT-15 targets sustained regrowth and grain production. Benefits from combining them would require testing rather than being assumed from either capability alone.

change_log.change: Preserved BOT-15 and its title while defining the proposed advance as broad transferability beyond existing productive perennial rice.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence already documents a substantial perennial staple-rice demonstration; presenting the first such rice as wholly prospective would misstate the baseline.

change_log.change: Added publication and trial dates, the reported yields of 6.8 versus 6.7 Mg ha−1 per harvest, site variation, fifth-year decline and the adjacent-plot comparison limitation.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the quantitative achievement while making its duration, comparison basis and scope explicit.

change_log.change: Integrated survival, regrowth, fertility, resource reserves, climate, disease and weed-management barriers into the explanation of the missing capability.
change_log.reason: Useful perennial grain production requires coordinated biological and agronomic performance rather than survival alone.

change_log.change: Qualified seed-versus-storage allocation and the proposed universal reversible master switch.
change_log.reason: The supplied review identifies no direct quantitative allocation result or demonstrated universal switch; neither uncertainty warrants removing the broader concept.

change_log.change: Separated reduced establishment from conditional economic, soil and climate consequences.
change_log.reason: Avoided establishment operations have a direct basis in the rice study, while broader benefits depend on management and environment. Soil carbon accumulation does not establish net climate benefit.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to cover more than one crop family, contrasting environments, independent reproduction and full multiyear comparisons.
change_log.reason: The evaluation should match the claimed breadth while remaining explicitly a proposal rather than a published standard or proof of universality.

change_log.change: Preserved partial extraction and missing supplementary-data limitations, and left subsequent progress unassessed.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports the paper's reported findings but cannot reconstruct all analyses or establish the field's later state.

change_log.change: Added distinctions from relevant roster concepts as explicitly labeled conceptual synthesis.
change_log.reason: Related capabilities may enable or complement perennial grains without establishing the same outcome; the supplied paper does not substantiate these roster comparisons.

unresolved_issues: The supplied record does not establish subsequent progress after the 2022 publication or whether the proposed breadth had been achieved by 1 November 2026.
Missing visual content, blank extracted pages and absent supplementary tables leave detailed reconstruction of the reported experiments unresolved.
The extent to which a common breeding or engineering approach can transfer across grain crop families and contrasting environments remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
The quantitative relationship between seed production and reserves needed for repeated regrowth is not directly established in the supplied review.
Long-term economic performance, stand replacement intervals and environmental outcomes beyond the demonstrated rice settings require further evidence.
No conserved reversible master switch is established by the supplied evidence; that limitation does not establish its worldwide absence or make such a mechanism necessary for success.

brief.title: Grain crops that regrow for years
possible: Farmers could plant grain once and harvest it for several years, with crops surviving harvest and growing back. Rice already does this in some settings. The goal is to make useful, repeated harvests reliably achievable across major grain crops and different growing environments.
why: Growing grain this way could reduce farmers’ planting work, costs and soil disturbance. In rice, regrowth avoids repeating seedling nurseries, ploughing and transplanting after each harvest. Extending those savings to other grains could change the work needed to keep farms productive.

sources.showed: They crossed cultivated Asian rice with a wild African relative that regrows after harvest. Repeated breeding produced rice that combined regrowth with grain production.
sources.quote:
These data collectively showed that the PR 
lines we developed had agronomic traits resembling domesticated AR 
yet retained from the perennial O. longistaminata parent the ability to 
regrow vigorously after harvest.
sources.cited_for: Rice demonstrates that useful grain production can coexist with repeated regrowth.
sources.not_established: The rice trials do not establish a transferable approach across grain crop families and contrasting environments.

sources.showed: A trial on a Minnesota farm compared intermediate wheatgrass, a grain crop that survives across years, with and without grazing. Grazing generated forage income but reduced total grain production.
sources.quote: Both agronomic systems generally displayed similar forage yields of comparable nutritive value.
sources.cited_for: Using a grain crop for grazing as well as grain changes its production and financial returns.
sources.not_established: This farm trial does not establish reliable yields or economic advantages across crops and environments.

shown: Shilai Zhang and colleagues reported that irrigated rice in Yunnan sustained grain production for four years after planting, with average yields per harvest similar to replanted annual rice. Performance varied by site, and yields fell significantly afterward.
missing: A reliable breeding or engineering approach still needs to work across grain crop families and contrasting environments.
Comparative trials need to establish lasting yields and full costs, including replacing declining crops.
Direct measurements need to establish where soil, erosion and climate benefits accompany practical gains for farmers.

milestones.label: Transfer across crop families and growing environments
milestones.explanation: Independent demonstrations would have to establish a shared approach across major grains from different crop families and contrasting environments. They would distinguish transferable features from crop-specific adaptations.

milestones.label: Repeated trials establish production and costs over several years
milestones.explanation: Repeated trials would compare survival, regrowth, fertility, harvest yields, total production and full costs against local annual crops, tracking variation, decline and replacement. This would test whether early gains last.

milestones.label: Measured farm and environmental benefits
milestones.explanation: Trials would measure labor, inputs, disease and weed management, soil, erosion, finances and the balance of greenhouse gases. This would establish where cultivation across years offers advantages over annual crops.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce the main farming results
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would reproduce the approach and main farming results using documented materials, methods and accessible data within stated growing conditions. This would establish how broadly the results hold.

uncertain: How much grain can plants produce while retaining enough stored resources to grow back repeatedly?
How will cold, heat, drought, disease and weeds affect productive crop life and replacement timing?
More soil carbon alone does not establish a climate benefit; methane and nitrous oxide emissions also affect the balance.
